lessons.title: ARC & Retain Counts
lessons.body:
Swift uses **Automatic Reference Counting (ARC)** to manage memory. The compiler analyzes your code at compile time and automatically inserts `retain` and `release` calls — you never write them yourself.

Every class instance has an internal **retain count**. When you create an instance, the count starts at 1. Each new strong reference increments it; each reference going away decrements it. When the count reaches **0**, ARC immediately calls `deinit` and frees the memory.

```swift
class Car {
    let model: String
    init(_ model: String) { self.model = model }
    deinit { print("\(model) deallocated") }
}

var first: Car? = Car("Tesla")  // retain count = 1
var second: Car? = first         // retain count = 2
first = nil                      // retain count = 1
second = nil                     // retain count = 0 → deinit called
```

This is fundamentally different from **garbage collection** (used by Java or Go). A garbage collector runs periodically on a separate thread and cleans up unreachable objects in batches — timing is non-deterministic. ARC is **deterministic**: deallocation happens the instant the last reference disappears, making resource cleanup predictable and tight.

Because ARC works at compile time rather than runtime, there is no GC pause or background scan. The trade-off is that ARC cannot automatically detect **retain cycles**, which you must handle yourself with `weak` and `unowned` references.

quickCheck.prompt: When does ARC call deinit on an object?
quickCheck.explanation: ARC tracks the retain count for every class instance. The moment that count reaches 0 — meaning no strong references remain — ARC immediately calls deinit and frees the memory.

options.text: When retain count drops to 0
When the app moves to background
After every function returns
At the end of the run loop

lessons.title: strong, weak, and unowned

quickCheck.prompt: What type must a `weak` variable be?
quickCheck.explanation: ARC automatically zeroes a weak reference when its target is deallocated. Optional is the correct type because the value can legitimately become nil at any point without programmer intervention.

options.text: Optional
non-Optional
AnyObject
Any

lessons.title: Retain Cycles & Closures

quickCheck.prompt: In a closure capture list, `[weak self]` makes self…
quickCheck.explanation: Capturing self as weak gives it Optional type inside the closure, allowing ARC to nil it out if the object is deallocated before the closure runs — preventing both a cycle and a crash.

options.text: Optional inside the closure
unowned
a strong reference
nil immediately

questions.prompt: What does ARC stand for, and what does it do?
questions.explanation: ARC analyzes object ownership at compile time and inserts retain/release calls, eliminating manual memory management while keeping deterministic deallocation timing.

options.text: Automatic Reference Counting — tracks object lifetimes and inserts retain/release automatically
Async Resource Control — manages async tasks
App Runtime Cache — caches frequently used objects
Automatic Resource Cleanup — releases unused resources in the run loop

questions.prompt: When should you use `unowned` instead of `weak`?
questions.explanation: `unowned` assumes the object is always alive when accessed; use it only when the closure's lifetime is strictly shorter than the object's, to avoid the Optional overhead of `weak`.

options.text: When the captured object may be nil at access time
When you are certain the captured object outlives the closure
Always — unowned is more performant
When the reference is to a struct

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: a.next holds b and b.next holds a — a strong cycle keeps both objects alive even after the variables are nil'd. Neither deinit is called.

options.text: deinit is never printed — retain cycle
deinit prints twice
deinit prints once
compile error

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to break a retain cycle in a stored closure property?
questions.explanation: A capture list prevents the closure from incrementing self's retain count, breaking the cycle and allowing deallocation.

options.text: Use [weak self] or [unowned self] in the closure capture list
Mark the closure @escaping
Declare the closure as a lazy var
Use a local variable instead of self

questions.explanation: `t` goes out of scope at the end of `test()`, so ARC calls deinit before `test()` returns — 'gone' prints before 'after'.

options.text: gone then after
after then gone
gone
nothing

questions.prompt: Value types (struct/enum) and ARC: which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: ARC tracks class instances only. Structs and enums are stored by value (on the stack or inline) and need no reference counting.

options.text: Value types are always reference-counted
Value types are not reference-counted; ARC applies to class instances
Value types use a separate reference counting system
Only enums with associated values are reference-counted

questions.prompt: Why must a `weak` reference always be declared as Optional?
questions.explanation: ARC zeroes a weak reference when its target is deallocated. Optional is the natural type for a value that can become nil at any time.

options.text: Because the compiler requires it for syntax
Because the object may be deallocated and ARC sets the reference to nil automatically
To allow the reference to be reassigned
Because weak references are stored on the heap

questions.prompt: In which scenario does `unowned` cause a crash?
questions.explanation: Accessing an `unowned` reference after the object has been deallocated is undefined behavior and triggers an immediate crash.

options.text: When the captured object is still alive
When the closure is stored longer than the captured object's lifetime
When used inside an actor
When the reference is to a struct

questions.explanation: `a.b` is weak, so B's retain count doesn't include that reference. When `b = nil`, the only strong ref to B is gone, and deinit fires.

options.text: Yes — B gone prints
No — retain cycle
compile error
runtime error

questions.prompt: Capturing `self` in an escaping closure stored as a property creates a retain cycle because…
questions.explanation: The cycle is: self.property → closure → self. Either side keeping the other alive prevents deallocation until the cycle is explicitly broken.

options.text: escaping closures always retain self strongly by default
self retains the closure (via the property) and the closure retains self (via capture) — both keep each other alive
the closure is reference-counted separately from self
Swift does not allow closures to capture self
